title: Salida Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Salida wells have a 100-ft median depth and 13 gpm median yield. See local costs, water levels, risks and permit history.
h1: What Salida Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well conditions around Salida vary with the mountain bedrock, drainage and lot location. The local permit record covers 2,759 wells within 5 miles, giving buyers a useful starting point: the median well is 100 feet deep, the median reported yield is 13 gallons per minute, and the median static water level is 45 feet below ground.

Those figures describe permitted wells, not a guarantee for a new hole. A property near Smeltertown, Poncha Springs or the valley floor may drill differently from a mountain-side lot. Before buying, compare nearby permits, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate access, geology and the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Salida’s well depths reflect fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
Salida’s wells are commonly completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 2,655 wells in the records identified that way. That usually means granite or gneiss conditions where water travels through fractures rather than a uniform layer. The median depth is 100 feet, and the middle half runs from 50 to 165 feet.

Nearly half of the wells, 48 percent, are under 100 feet. Another 43 percent fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 8 percent are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 790 feet. For a bid, nearby well depths are more useful than a county-wide assumption. A 50-to-165-foot middle range still leaves room for a much deeper hole on a difficult fractured-rock lot.

sections.heading: Most Salida wells make usable household water
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a solid local result for ordinary household use, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed long-term production. A well test and the driller’s completion report matter more than a nearby headline number.

About 60 percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 35 percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1 percent are under 1 gallon per minute, while 4 percent are between 1 and 5. Low-yield wells can still work with storage, but they deserve careful design and a clear discussion of household demand. Exempt household-use wells also have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels in Salida vary without a simple decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 45 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 25 to 80 feet. This is the water level measured when the well is at rest, not necessarily the level while pumping. A shallow static level does not by itself prove that a well will produce strongly.

The decade figures do not show a steady downward trend. Median depth to water was 30 feet in the 1970s, 72 feet in the 1990s, 40 feet in the 2000s, 53 feet in the 2010s and 40 feet in the 2020s. These measurements come from different wells and locations, so treat them as local context rather than a site-specific forecast. Ask for the actual static and pumping levels on any well you may buy.

sections.heading: Salida’s permit history shows continuing drilling activity
sections.html:
Domestic and household wells make up 83 percent of the local permit use mix. Stock wells account for 6 percent, irrigation for 2 percent and monitoring for 4 percent. The record includes 1,879 constructed wells, while 2,129 report a total depth and 1,153 report a pump yield. Those differences matter: not every permit contains the same level of construction or performance information.

Permit activity increased from 46 in the 1950s and 47 in the 1960s to 283 in the 1970s, 534 in the 1990s and 572 in the 2000s. The newest permit year is 2026. The most frequent drillers in the records are American Drilling Service, Mccoy Drilling Inc and M & M Backhoe Service. A permit record is useful evidence, but verify current licensing and availability before hiring.

sections.heading: A typical Salida well budget starts near $12,500
sections.html:
Local drilling conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite or gneiss. The modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the median depth of 100 feet, the drilled hole alone models at about $6,500 to $10,000.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at approximately $12,500 to $22,000. That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. Access for a rig, casing and grout requirements, difficult rock, extra depth and the distance to the building can change the price. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing, completion, pump equipment, electrical and trenching. On a steep lot near Salida, site access can affect the budget before drilling begins.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic layout and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves attention before closing. Within about 10 miles, the map shows 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 618 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are reasons to review site history and test the water. Historic mining can also raise questions about metals and other contaminants.

Low yield and a dry hole remain practical risks in fractured rock, even where nearby wells perform well. Have the well location, septic area, driveway and building envelope considered together. Keep required separation between the well and septic system, protect the wellhead from surface drainage, and confirm that the lot can support the intended construction. A water test after completion is part of responsible due diligence, not a substitute for checking the surrounding land uses.

sections.heading: Use nearby permits before buying a Salida lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the property, including records around Smeltertown and Poncha Springs when they are relevant to the site. Compare reported depth, yield, static water level, aquifer description and use. A cluster of shallow wells can support a reasonable drilling estimate, but it cannot guarantee the same fracture will be encountered on your lot.

Before building, confirm the well permit path with Colorado DWR and determine whether the proposed household use is allowed. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for the intended use. Ask a driller to walk the site and price access, drilling, casing, grout, pump, trenching and electrical separately. For a purchase, make water rights, permit status, construction records, pumping performance and laboratory testing conditions in the contract.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Salida, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well within 5 miles of Salida is 100 feet deep. The middle half runs from 50 to 165 feet. About 48 percent are under 100 feet, while 43 percent are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce much deeper wells; the deepest record reaches 790 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Salida?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at $6,500 to $10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000. Access, depth and completion details can move the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Salida?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 60 percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 1 percent report under 1 gallon per minute. A pumping test is still needed for a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Salida?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a neighboring well. The area has 10 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 618 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test a private well after completion and review nearby mining and environmental history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Do I need to check a well permit before buying near Salida?
faq.a: Yes. The local records include 2,759 permitted wells, but only 1,879 are recorded as constructed and 1,153 report a pump yield. Review the actual permit, construction report, use, yield and static water level. Confirm the proposed use with Colorado DWR, especially if an augmentation plan may apply in an over-appropriated basin.
